title: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions by Whole Numbers
summary: Learn how to estimate, multiply and divide proper fractions by whole numbers, with diagrams that show why the rules work, worked Checkpoint-style examples and a 14-question practice quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Estimate the answer, then multiply a proper fraction by a whole number, e.g. 3/4 × 5 (6Nf.06)
Estimate the answer, then divide a proper fraction by a whole number, e.g. 3/4 ÷ 2 (6Nf.06)
Write answers in simplest form and as mixed numbers when the answer is bigger than 1 — skills from Simplest Form (6Nf.03) that Checkpoint expects you to use here

blocks.text: In this lesson you learn two short rules — one for multiplying and one for dividing — and, more importantly, **why** they work. A proper fraction is a fraction smaller than 1, like 3/4 or 2/7. Here we only multiply or divide it by a **whole number** (2, 3, 12 …). Checkpoint tests this on Paper 1 (no calculator), so you must be able to do it by hand quickly and check your answer with an estimate.
Key words

items: numerator
البسط — the top number; it counts how many parts you have
denominator
المقام — the bottom number; it tells you the size of each part (how many equal parts make 1 whole)
proper fraction
كسر حقيقي — numerator smaller than denominator, e.g. 5/8 (less than 1)
improper fraction
كسر غير حقيقي — numerator equal to or bigger than denominator, e.g. 15/4 (1 or more)
mixed number
عدد كسري — a whole number and a fraction together, e.g. 3 3/4
simplest form
أبسط صورة — numerator and denominator have no common factor except 1, e.g. 6/8 → 3/4
product
حاصل الضرب — the answer to a multiplication
quotient
خارج القسمة — the answer to a division
estimate
تقدير — a quick, rounded answer to check that the real answer is sensible

blocks.text: 1. Multiplying a fraction by a whole number
Multiplication is **repeated addition**. 2/7 × 3 means 'three lots of 2/7': 2/7 + 2/7 + 2/7. The parts are all sevenths, so you just count the sevenths: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 sevenths.

blocks.text: So the rule is: **multiply the numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator the same.** The denominator only names the size of the pieces, and multiplying does not change the size of the pieces.

items: **Estimate** first: is the fraction near 0, near 1/2 or near 1? (see section 3)
Multiply the **numerator** by the whole number. Keep the **denominator**.
If the answer is an improper fraction, change it to a **mixed number**: divide the numerator by the denominator; the remainder is the new numerator.
Write the fraction part in its **simplest form**.
Compare with your estimate.

blocks.title: Order does not matter
blocks.text: 3 × 2/5 and 2/5 × 3 give the same answer (6/5), just like 3 × 4 = 4 × 3. Also, 2/3 × 12 is the same as '2/3 of 12' — you can find 1/3 of 12 (= 4) and double it (= 8). Use whichever way is easier.
2. Dividing a fraction by a whole number
Division is **sharing into equal groups**. 4/5 ÷ 2 means 'share 4 fifths between 2'. Each group gets 2 fifths.

blocks.caption: 4/5 ÷ 2 = 2/5: four fifths shared equally into 2 groups gives 2 fifths in each group.

blocks.text: **Case A — the numerator divides exactly:** divide the numerator and keep the denominator. 4/5 ÷ 2 = 2/5, 9/10 ÷ 3 = 3/10, 8/9 ÷ 4 = 2/9.

**Case B — the numerator does not divide exactly** (for example 3/4 ÷ 2: you cannot share 3 quarters equally into 2 groups of whole quarters). Cut every part into 2 smaller equal parts. Quarters become eighths, and each group gets 3 eighths.

blocks.text: So the general rule is: **keep the numerator and multiply the denominator by the whole number.** This rule always works — even in Case A. For example 4/5 ÷ 2 = 4/10, and 4/10 simplifies to 2/5, the same answer as before.

items: **Estimate**: the answer must be **smaller** than the fraction you started with.
If the numerator divides exactly by the whole number, divide it and keep the denominator.
Otherwise, keep the numerator and **multiply the denominator** by the whole number.
Simplify if you can.
Check by multiplying back: answer × whole number should give the starting fraction.

blocks.title: Dividing by 3 is the same as finding one third
blocks.text: 3/4 ÷ 3 is the same as 1/3 of 3/4. Dividing by 2 is halving, dividing by 4 is finding a quarter. Word problems often say 'half of', 'a third of' or 'shared equally between' — all of these mean divide.
3. Estimating before you calculate

The curriculum asks you to **estimate** as well as calculate. Compare the fraction with the 'friendly' fractions 0, 1/2 and 1. A fraction is near 1/2 when the numerator is about half of the denominator (4/9, 5/9), and near 1 when the numerator is almost as big as the denominator (7/8, 9/10).

rows: 7/8 is nearly 1, so a little less than 11
5/9 is just over 1/2, so just over 4
the answer must be less than 4/5, about a quarter of it

items: proper fraction × whole number → the answer is **smaller than the whole number** (you take only part of it each time).
proper fraction ÷ whole number → the answer is **smaller than the fraction** you started with.
If your answer breaks one of these facts, check your working again.

blocks.title: القاعدة اللي لازم تحفظها
blocks.text: في الضرب: اضرب البسط بس في العدد الصحيح والمقام زي ما هو (لأن حجم الجزء ماتغيرش، عدد الأجزاء بس اللي زاد). مثال: 2/7 × 3 = 6/7. في القسمة: البسط زي ما هو واضرب المقام في العدد الصحيح (لأنك بتقطع كل جزء لقطع أصغر). مثال: 3/4 ÷ 2 = 3/8. ولو البسط بيقبل القسمة، ممكن تقسمه على طول: 4/5 ÷ 2 = 2/5. وفي الآخر بسّط الكسر وحوّله لعدد كسري لو أكبر من 1.
4. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Work out 3/8 × 6. Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form. [2]

items: Estimate: 3/8 is a bit less than 1/2, so the answer is a bit less than 3.
Multiply the numerator: 3 × 6 = 18, so 3/8 × 6 = 18/8.
Change to a mixed number: 18 ÷ 8 = 2 remainder 2, so 18/8 = 2 2/8.
Simplify: 2/8 = 1/4. **Answer: 2 1/4** — a bit less than 3 ✓

blocks.text: Common mistake: stopping at 2 2/8. The question says simplest form, so 2 2/8 would lose the second mark.
**Worked example 2** — Work out 6/7 ÷ 3. [1]
6 divides exactly by 3: 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Keep the sevenths. **Answer: 2/7.** Check: 2/7 × 3 = 6/7 ✓. (Using the general rule, 6/21 also simplifies to 2/7.)
**Worked example 3** — Work out 2/3 ÷ 5. [1]

2 does not divide by 5, so keep the numerator and multiply the denominator: 3 × 5 = 15. **Answer: 2/15.** Check: 2/15 × 5 = 10/15 = 2/3 ✓. Common mistake: writing 10/3 (multiplying the numerator) — that makes the answer bigger, which is impossible when you divide.
**Worked example 4** — Ring the best estimate for 7/8 × 11.   5   8   10   13 [1]
7/8 is very close to 1, so 7/8 × 11 is a little less than 11. **Ring 10.** (13 is too big — more than 11 is impossible; 5 would be the estimate for 1/2 × 11.) The exact answer is 77/8 = 9 5/8.
**Worked example 5** — A jug holds 3/4 litre of juice. Amira pours all of it equally into 6 glasses. What fraction of a litre is in each glass? [2]

items: 'Equally into 6 glasses' means divide: 3/4 ÷ 6.
3 does not divide by 6, so multiply the denominator: 3/24.
Simplify (÷ 3): 3/24 = 1/8. **Answer: 1/8 litre.**

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Omar says 4/5 ÷ 2 = 4/10. Sara says 4/5 ÷ 2 = 2/5. Who is correct? Explain your answer. [1]

**Both are correct.** 4/10 and 2/5 are equivalent fractions (divide the numerator and denominator of 4/10 by 2 to get 2/5). Omar used 'multiply the denominator', Sara used 'divide the numerator'. Sara's answer is in its simplest form. This is the kind of convincing (TWM) answer Checkpoint likes: say who is right and give the mathematical reason.
**Worked example 7** — Write the missing number: 2/5 × ☐ = 2 2/5 [1]
Change the mixed number to an improper fraction: 2 2/5 = 10/5 + 2/5 = 12/5. The denominator stays 5, so 2 × ☐ = 12, ☐ = **6**. Check: 2/5 × 6 = 12/5 = 2 2/5 ✓

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Multiplying both numbers: 2/7 × 3 = 6/21 ✗. That is just an equivalent fraction of 2/7 — nothing was multiplied! Correct: 6/7.
Dividing the denominator: 3/4 ÷ 2 = 3/2 ✗. Dividing must make the fraction smaller. Correct: 3/8.
Leaving an improper fraction or an unsimplified answer when the question asks for a mixed number in simplest form (18/8 instead of 2 1/4).
Wrong remainder when changing to a mixed number: 15/4 = 3 3/4, not 3 1/4. Check: 3 × 4 + 3 = 15 ✓.
Not reading the word problem: 'shared equally', 'each', 'a third of' → divide; 'how much altogether in 12 bottles' → multiply.
Not checking with an estimate: an answer like 3/8 × 6 = 18 should look wrong at once, because 3/8 × 6 must be less than 6.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: Short calculations with an answer box: 'Work out 5/6 × 4. Give your answer as a mixed number.' Read the last sentence — it tells you the form of the answer.
Missing-number boxes: 3/8 × ☐ = 15/8 or 4/9 ÷ ☐ = 4/27. Use the inverse: what was the numerator or denominator multiplied by?
Ring or tick the best estimate — compare the fraction with 0, 1/2 and 1.
Word problems (ribbons, juice, recipes, distances) — decide multiply or divide first and write the calculation down: it can earn a method mark even if the arithmetic slips.
'Explain' or 'Who is correct?' questions — give a reason using maths words: 'dividing makes it smaller', 'the denominator shows the size of the parts', 'these fractions are equivalent'.
These questions usually appear on Paper 1 (no calculator), so practise doing them by hand. Show your working in the space given.

blocks.title: إزاي تتأكد من إجابتك
blocks.text: اسأل نفسك سؤالين: هل الإجابة منطقية؟ كسر أقل من 1 مضروب في عدد صحيح لازم يدي أقل من العدد ده. وكسر مقسوم على عدد صحيح لازم يصغر. وبعدين اعمل العملية العكسية: لو قسمت، اضرب الإجابة في العدد الصحيح ولازم يرجع لك الكسر الأصلي.
Practice

blocks.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. No calculator. Give fractions as a/b (for example 3/8). For mixed numbers type a space, e.g. 2 1/4. Write your working on paper first.

questions.e: Multiply the numerator only: 3 × 3 = 9. The denominator stays 10 (the pieces are still tenths). 3/10 × 3 = **9/10**. (9/30 is wrong: it multiplies the denominator too.)

questions.q: Without working out the exact answer, explain why 5/8 × 7 must be less than 7 but more than 3.
questions.ms: 1 mark: 5/8 is less than 1, so 5/8 × 7 is less than 1 × 7 = 7 (oe, e.g. 'you are taking less than the whole of 7'). 1 mark: 5/8 is more than 1/2 (4/8), so the answer is more than 1/2 × 7 = 3.5, which is more than 3. Accept the exact answer 35/8 = 4 3/8 used as a check only if a reason is also given.

questions.q: Work out 5/6 × 3. Give your answer as a mixed number in its simplest form.

questions.e: 8 can be divided by 4: 8 ÷ 4 = 2, denominator stays 9. 8/9 ÷ 4 = **2/9**. Check: 2/9 × 4 = 8/9 ✓
3 cannot be divided by 4 exactly, so multiply the denominator by 4: 5 × 4 = 20. 3/5 ÷ 4 = **3/20**. Check: 3/20 × 4 = 12/20 = 3/5 ✓

questions.q: Which is the best estimate for 9/10 × 21?
questions.e: 9/10 is just under 1, so the answer is just under 21. 19 is the only choice a little less than 21. (Exact: 189/10 = 18.9.)
The numerator stayed 5, so the denominator was multiplied by the whole number: 6 × ☐ = 24. 24 ÷ 6 = **4**.

questions.q: A ribbon is 4/5 m long. Huda cuts it into 8 equal pieces. What fraction of a metre is each piece? Give your answer in its simplest form.
questions.e: 4/5 ÷ 8: 4 cannot be divided by 8 exactly, so multiply the denominator: 4/40. Simplify (÷ 4): 4/40 = **1/10 m**. (M1 for 4/5 ÷ 8 or 4/40.) Check: 1/10 × 8 = 8/10 = 4/5 ✓

questions.q: A bottle holds 2/3 litre of water. How many litres of water are in 12 full bottles?
Which calculation has an answer greater than 3?
Mona writes: 3/4 ÷ 2 = 3/2. Explain her mistake and write the correct answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a correct explanation, e.g. she divided the denominator by 2 instead of multiplying it by 2 / her answer 3/2 is bigger than 3/4 but dividing by 2 must make it smaller / halving quarters gives eighths. 1 mark: 3/8 cao.
questions.e: Dividing a proper fraction by a whole number makes it smaller, but 3/2 = 1 1/2 is bigger than 3/4. Mona divided the 4 by 2. Halve each quarter to make eighths: 3/4 ÷ 2 = **3/8**.

questions.p:
Question 14
A recipe for one cake uses 3/4 of a cup of sugar.
questions.q: (a) How many cups of sugar are needed for 6 cakes?

questions.p:
Question 14
A recipe for one cake uses 3/4 of a cup of sugar.
questions.q: (b) Laila makes a small cake that needs one third of the sugar for one cake. What fraction of a cup of sugar does she use?
questions.e: One third of 3/4 means 3/4 ÷ 3. 3 ÷ 3 = 1, so 3/4 ÷ 3 = **1/4 cup**.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Fraction × whole number: multiply the numerator, keep the denominator (2/7 × 3 = 6/7).
Fraction ÷ whole number: keep the numerator, multiply the denominator (3/4 ÷ 2 = 3/8) — or divide the numerator if it divides exactly (4/5 ÷ 2 = 2/5).
Change improper answers to mixed numbers and always simplify.
Estimate with 0, 1/2 and 1: proper fraction × 11 is less than 11; dividing always makes a proper fraction smaller.
Check division by multiplying back.
